Most people using Nix on Red Hat/Debian/Ubuntu use it to install package versions their distro lacks or to link against different library versions. Nix 'makes the dreaded autotools dance much more bearable, even for someone like me who doesn't really know any C++.'

For multi-language dev projects with overlapping but incompatible dependencies (e.g. Python libs needing specific C library versions), where virtualenv-style tools fail, the commenter finds Nix ideal. They describe Docker/docker-compose as slower and likely to break months later.

Configuring everything with the Nix language on NixOS varies a lot. Obscure packages often didn't expose enough configuration, forcing the user to make their own version, which is 'pretty annoying and time consuming.' Nixpkgs maintainers 'get a lot of work done... but there just aren't enough of them yet.'

Configuring popular software like Nginx and Postgres is often much easier in the Nix language. Small syntax errors are harder to make, templating helps, and you can reuse constants across config files. Configuring systemd services on NixOS is 'really well handled.'

NixOS modules merge configuration elegantly; for example, user lists from multiple modules get combined. Compare Arch, where updated defaults land in .pacnew files that are easy to miss. 'My arch system has 22 .pacnew files in /etc, and occasionally things break.'

A skeptic reacting to how config works in Nix: having to write a Nix package and learn the language just to modify global config files 'sounds like an absolute nightmare for a local machine, though possibly a great tool for automated systems.'
'I really love the temporary installs feature' of Nix. It's handy for trying software once without accumulating bloat from forgotten uninstalls.
Temporary installs still stay in the store until garbage collection: 'My record with nix-collect-garbage was like 30 GB. I since enable the auto-gc.'

Most apps listed as Homebrew-only (Android Studio, tealdeer, Heroku CLI, Sublime Text, Slack, Postman) are in Nixpkgs. Nix can run on top of any Linux distro, separate from the base system, like brew on macOS. The caveat: 'You won't like the CLI though.'

Building lots of Docker images with Nix is 'generally more pleasant than using Dockerfiles.' However, the 128 layer limit is 'really annoying and easy to hit,' and the workaround of grouping store paths makes poor use of storage and bandwidth.

nix2container is 'truly magical' for large multi-layer containers: it never rebuilds or reuploads an unchanged layer. 'All the existing methods for grouping store paths into layers are finnicky, brittle, and non-optimal.'

With nixpkgs' automatic layering, the last layer becomes a clump of leftover dependencies. Using nix2container, the commenter manually layered Python, then app dependencies, then the app, so a bugfix only replaces a few-KB final layer.
For gradual adoption, you can keep a Dockerfile that builds the Nix configuration and reuse existing Docker infrastructure. The downside is that you don't take advantage of layers at all.
Nixpkgs should reduce package count. Waiting 2 days for unbound CVE patch merge is unbearable.

In practice the commenter found NixOS annoying: a static system that restricts problem solving. They call Nix 'ugly to no ends' and question the need for a new language. Hashed store directories are unreadable compared to something like /Programs/Python/3.15.0/.

The commenter can manage NixOS given their background, but sees very low chance a standard office worker would be happy moving from Windows to it. HN Nix purists 'gloss over all the warts that has kept this ecosystem from growing much.'
'I really liked how easy it was to create a custom ISO' with Nix. Dvorak as default keyboard, neovim, and needed proprietary WiFi drivers all came from a minimal config file and `nix build`.

The commenter wants to adopt Nix/NixOS, but 'the cost of wrapping packages is just a little too high for me right now.' Still, they consider Nix's hermetic dependency-closure image builds far superior security-wise to writing Dockerfiles.
Reproducible NixOS builds mean everyone building it gets the exact same binary, so you can trust any source by verifying the hash. The commenter calls it 'a pretty big deal.'
The 100% reproducible minimal ISO was reportedly achieved by removing Python bytecode from the builds, which has a performance hit and 'should probably be reverted.'
